title: How Roman doctors seem to contradict themselves: divine-faith doubt vs conjectural certainty
source_text: XXV. Unde patet quomodo secum sint conciliandi Ecclesiae Romanae Doctores, qui in hac quaestione loqui videntur repugnantia & contradictoria. Quando enim nostrorum argumentis respondent, aut hujus controversiae statum explicant, atque constituunt, negant se fidelibus tollere omnem de propria gratia certitudinem; concedunt illos esse posse de sua coram Deo justificatione vere persuados, certos, & securos; neque necessarium esse ut de remissione peccatorum suorum perpetuo haesitent, fluctuent, & dubitent: Et tamen quando contra nos disputant, aut apud plebem suam concionantur, multis argumentis probare contendunt fideles circa propriam justitiam dubios & incertos esse, nescire an sint in Dei gratia; nec illos nisi temere, posse certo & absque dubitatione statuere, peccatorum remissionem se per Christum esse consecutos. Verum quum affirmant fideles & justos nescire an sint in Dei gratia, neque id certo cognoscere & judicare posse, loquuntur de certitudine quam vocant fidei divinae, aut de ea saltem quae omnem formidinem oppositae partis excludit; non vero de conjecturali illa certitudine, quae opponitur quidem proprie dictae dubitationi, & significat verum & determinatum assensum alterius partis contradictionis, sed quae tamen cum aliqua formidine consistere potest. Et quum fidelibus tribuunt aliquam dubitationem de sua apud Deum gratia atque justitia, per id non intelligunt proprie dictam dubitationem, sive haesitationem & fluctuationem mentis, quae neutri parti contradictionis assentiri & accedere audet, sed dubitationem solum latius sumptam, quae consistit cum judicio mentis fixo atque determinato, & dicit solum aliquam formidinem oppositae partis. Quamvis enim, inquit Vasquez, cum assensu determinato alterius partis per propria principia, non possit esse dubitatio inter utramque partem per eadem principia, bene tamen potest esse formido illa quam diximus, per principia extrinseca & universalia, per quae intelligimus posse rem illam aliter se habere, & fortassis aliter tunc esse quam opinamur; quae sane formido videtur esse genus quoddam dubitationis. Cap. illo nono jam citato, ubi pluribus rem illam explicat.
pass_a_gloss: Hence it is plain how the doctors of the Roman Church are to be reconciled with themselves, who on this question seem to speak things repugnant and contradictory. For when they answer our arguments, or explain and settle the state of this controversy, they deny that they take away from the faithful every certainty concerning their own grace; they grant that those can be truly persuaded, certain, and secure concerning their justification before God; and that it is not necessary that they perpetually hesitate, fluctuate, and doubt concerning the remission of their sins: And yet when they dispute against us, or preach among their people, they contend with many arguments to prove that the faithful are doubtful and uncertain concerning their own righteousness, do not know whether they are in God’s grace; and that only rashly can they certainly and without doubt establish that they have obtained remission of sins through Christ. But when they affirm that the faithful and just do not know whether they are in God’s grace, and cannot certainly know and judge it, they speak of the certainty which they call of divine faith, or at least of that which excludes every fear of the opposite side; not of that conjectural certainty which is indeed opposed to doubt properly so called, and signifies a true and determinate assent to one side of the contradiction, but which can nevertheless consist with some fear. And when they attribute to the faithful some doubt concerning their grace and righteousness with God, by that they do not understand doubt properly so called, or hesitation and fluctuation of mind which dares assent and approach neither side of the contradiction, but only doubt more broadly taken, which consists with a fixed and determinate judgment of the mind, and means only some fear of the opposite side. For although, says Vasquez, with determinate assent to one side through proper principles there cannot be doubt between both sides through the same principles, yet well can there be that fear which we have mentioned, through extrinsic and universal principles by which we understand that that thing can be otherwise, and perhaps then is otherwise than we think; which fear indeed seems to be a certain kind of doubt. In that ninth chapter already cited, where he explains that matter at greater length.
pass_b_english: Roman polemic sounds self-contradictory: sometimes allowing certainty, sometimes calling the faithful doubtful.
The key is equivocation—denying divine-faith certainty while granting conjectural certainty, and calling residual fear ‘doubt’ in a broad sense.
